gree-004.title: Farming begins in the Fertile Crescent
gree-004.text: Barley was among the first crops: it was domesticated in the Near East around 11,000 years ago. The warming from 11.7 ka coincides with the earliest farming in the Fertile Crescent. In that arc of land, crop growing and herding opened the Neolithic, the farming phase of the Stone Age. Its first farmers tamed sheep, goats, cattle and later pigs, along with cereals such as wheat and barley, and legumes. Domesticated emmer wheat appears in Iran by 9,800 BP. Between 8500 and 7000 BC people across the region took up the systematic husbandry of plants and animals. The new way of life also travelled by sea: Neolithic settlers had reached Cyprus by 8800–8600 BC. A milder climate after {{ref:gree-005}} made the change possible, and from here it spread, as {{ref:gree-029}} shows.

gree-005.title: The Younger Dryas ends and the Holocene begins
gree-005.text: Greenland's average yearly temperature rose by about 8 °C within 40 years. The jump came in three steps of five years each. It ended the Younger Dryas, a cold spell that began about 12,800 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. Its close also closed the Last Glacial Period and the Pleistocene, and opened the Holocene, the epoch people still live in. Geologists mark that boundary with a GSSP, a reference point fixed in rock or ice. Here it is a sample in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland, matched to the end of the Younger Dryas and ratified in 2008. After the sudden jump, global warming continued at a somewhat gentler pace through the Greenlandian. Earth has stayed in this interglacial ever since. In the American Southwest, the cool, wet pluvial climate gave way to semi-arid conditions.

gree-009.title: Northern ice sheets melt fast
gree-009.text: Most of the ice-sheet melting and sea-level rise of the last deglaciation came after about 11,000 years ago. The trigger was the abrupt warming that opened the Holocene, around 9700 BC, which set off rapid melting of the remaining ice sheets in North America and Europe. An ice sheet's surface mass balance is its yearly gain of snow minus its loss to melting. For the Laurentide ice sheet it turned negative only in the early Holocene, once radiative forcing and summer temperatures rose. In northern British Columbia, the Cordilleran ice sheet had essentially melted away by about 11,000 years ago. Later, from 8,500 BP, ice pouring from the collapsing Laurentide ice sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic.

gree-020.title: The first livestock: goats, sheep, pigs and cattle
gree-020.text: By 10,000 years ago, hunters were culling young males and sparing females to breed. That simple choice marks the slide from hunting to herding. Zooarchaeology is the study of animal remains from human sites. It shows that goats, pigs, sheep and taurine cattle were the first livestock, domesticated in the Fertile Crescent 11,000–10,000 years ago. The earliest dates in northern Mesopotamia are c. 9000 BCE for goats and sheep, c. 8500 BCE for pigs and c. 8000 BCE for cattle. The milder climate after the Younger Dryas made it possible. Domestication began a rapid shift in the evolution, ecology and demography of people and of many animal and plant species. It brought a cost too: in Eurasia, domestic animals overtook other primates as the main source of new human infections.

nort-001.title: The 8.2-kiloyear cold snap
nort-001.text: In Greenland, the temperature fell 3.3 °C below the decadal average in under 20 years. Around 8,200 years ago global temperatures dropped abruptly, and the cool spell lasted two to four centuries; its coldest phase lasted about 60 years. The likely cause was a flood of fresh water. A meltwater pulse, probably from glacial lakes Agassiz and Ojibway draining into the North Atlantic, may have weakened Atlantic overturning by 55–62%. That overturning is the ocean circulation that carries warm surface water north, so slowing it chilled the lands around the Atlantic. The event shows up far beyond the North Atlantic. Cave records from Eurasia to South America and southern Africa show it. Methane fell 15%, and North and East Africa turned drier. Its signal in the NGRIP1 Greenland ice core is the GSSP for the base of the Northgrippian, set at 8,236 years before 2000. The drainage itself is told in {{ref:nort-002}}.

nort-002.title: Lakes Agassiz and Ojibway drain into the sea
nort-002.text: The final drainage of one giant North American lake raised global sea level by an estimated 0.8 to 2.8 m. As the last ice over Hudson Bay melted, Lake Agassiz drained almost completely in its final major drainage shift. Neighbouring Lake Ojibway, comparable in size, likely drained at the same time, perhaps in two floods through a broken ice dam and beneath the ice. This freshwater flood is the leading suspected trigger of {{ref:nort-001}}. The lake had a long history before its end. It refilled as the ice withdrew north of today's Canada–US border around 10,000 years ago, and abandoned its southern outlet by about 9400 BP.

nort-004.title: The Storegga Slides send a tsunami across the North Atlantic
nort-004.text: Tsunami sand in Scotland lies up to 29 km inland and 4 m above today's normal tide level. It came from Norway. There, three submarine landslides at the edge of the continental shelf moved about 3,500 km³ of debris along 290 km of shelf, among the largest known. An earthquake that destabilised methane clathrate, an icy solid that traps methane in seabed mud, is thought to have triggered the collapse. The slides set off large tsunamis, and waves up to 20 m high hit Scotland and the Faroe Islands. The tsunami may also have flooded Doggerland's last low-lying land, though its impact there is debated.

nort-005.title: Did early farmers warm the planet?
nort-005.text: Carbon dioxide rose markedly from about 8,000 years ago, and methane some 3,000 years later. William Ruddiman argues that forest clearing by early farmers caused that rise in greenhouse gases. If he is right, human influence on climate began long before industry. Other researchers challenge the idea. Critics counter with data from an earlier interglacial, and say all interglacials differ.

nort-008.title: The Holocene's warmest centuries
nort-008.text: The warmest 200 years of the Holocene, around 6,500 years ago, were about 0.7 °C warmer than the 19th century. The climate had recovered from the cold snap of {{ref:nort-001}} and climbed to the highest temperatures of the epoch. The warm phase reached its thermal maximum around 8,000 years BP, and polar ice caps shrank to their Holocene minimum. Rain belts moved with the heat. Tibet's Yarlung Tsangpo valley got up to twice today's rainfall, and a stable climate fostered farming in China. The peak did not last. The warmth was followed by a slow decline of 0.1–0.3 °C per millennium until about two centuries ago, a long cooling traced in {{ref:nort-022}}. Only the warming described in {{ref:megh-090}} broke that trend.

nort-009.title: The last steppe bison
nort-009.text: The steppe bison, a grazer of the mammoth steppe, survived in north-central eastern Siberia until about 8,000 years ago. Traces may stretch later. Bison DNA in northeastern Siberian permafrost may extend its survival to 5050–3800 BCE. The youngest North American remains, from Yukon, date to 3628–3377 BCE.

nort-010.title: Menengai collapses in Kenya's Rift Valley
nort-010.text: Menengai is a shield volcano, a broad, gently sloping cone, on the floor of Kenya's Rift Valley. About 8,000 years ago it collapsed to form its 12 × 8 km caldera, the bowl left when a volcano's summit falls in. The eruption is listed at VEI 6, with about 70 km³ of material.

nort-011.title: Rising seas cut off Tasmania and New Guinea
nort-011.text: Aboriginal Tasmanians had walked to their land across a land bridge about 40,000 years ago. Post-glacial sea-level rise then flooded the Bassian Plain, forming Bass Strait, making Tasmania an island and cutting its people off from the mainland. To the north, New Guinea separated from mainland Australia about 8,000 years ago, ending Sahul, the single landmass they had formed. The New Guinea land bridge was fully flooded by then. Over the next 2,000 years, thousands of Torres Strait and coastal islands formed.

nort-006.title: The Laurentide Ice Sheet's final collapse
nort-006.text: Central Asia stayed at near-glacial temperatures until a North American ice sheet collapsed around 8,000 BP. About 8,000 years ago the Laurentide Ice Sheet thinned and split into two lobes, over Quebec–Labrador and Keewatin. Its final melting came between 8 and 7 ka. After it, global sea level rose at a much slower rate. Ice discharge from the collapsing sheet made North Atlantic climate erratic until 6,700 BP. Ice finally left Nunavik about 6,500 years ago, ending the long retreat that began in {{ref:gree-009}}.

nort-012.title: The Mississippi and Rhine deltas take shape
nort-012.text: Deltas need a steady sea to grow. As sea-level rise slowed, the modern Mississippi River delta plain began to build around 8,000–7,500 years ago. In the Netherlands, the Holocene Rhine–Meuse delta began forming about 8,000 years ago, shaped by sea-level rise and tectonic subsidence. By switching course every 1,000–1,500 years, the Mississippi built six delta complexes. Such deltas became major farming and population centres.

nort-013.title: The last Irish elk
nort-013.text: The Irish elk, or giant deer, survived in western Russia until around 7,700 years ago, as Ice Age megafauna losses continued. By the early Holocene its range had shrunk dramatically. Its youngest eastern records, near Lake Baikal, date to 10,700–10,400 BP. Its latest dated remains include finds at Kamyshlov and Maloarkhangelsk, Russia, from the 6th millennium BCE, and it likely died out soon after.

nort-014.title: Mount Mazama blows apart and leaves Crater Lake
nort-014.text: A 48 km ash column reached the stratosphere when Oregon's Mount Mazama, active again after 20,000 quiet years, ended in a VEI 7 eruption. Its collapse left the caldera that now holds Crater Lake. The USGS has called it the largest explosive eruption in the Cascades in the past million years. Ash fell across eight western US states and three Canadian provinces. The orange Mazama Ash covers at least 900,000 km² of the northern Great Plains and reaches Greenland's ice sheet, making it a standard dating marker. Its aerosols may have cooled mid- to high northern latitudes by 0.6–0.7 °C for one to three years. Ashfall drove people out, leaving one Alberta site empty for about 200 years.

nort-015.title: Farming spreads into Europe
nort-015.text: Farming took about 2,500 years, 8500–6000 BP, to travel from the Aegean to Britain. It appears in the Aegean by c. 6500 BCE, and the Baltic followed around 5500 BP. Fast sea-level rise, the 8.2 ka cooling and loss of coastal land may have helped push this Neolithic Revolution into Europe. In Central Europe, human impact first shows in pollen records from 7,500 BP and becomes substantial after 6,300 BP. An Early Neolithic lakeshore village at La Marmotta, Italy, dates to about 5700 BC. From about 7,500 years ago, European Neolithic farmers also crossed from Iberia into Northwest Africa.

nort-016.title: Sundaland's last lowlands go under
nort-016.text: The Gulf of Thailand was dry, arid land before 7,500 BP. A marine transgression, the sea advancing over land, drowned it from 7,500 to 6,200 BP. It was part of Sundaland, the exposed Sunda Shelf of Southeast Asia, flooded as rising seas followed the 8.2 ka cool period. Its partial submergence, under way since 18,000 years ago, continued until about 5000 BC.

nort-017.title: Megatherium, the giant ground sloth, dies out
nort-017.text: Megatherium americanum was a ground sloth of up to 4 tonnes and 6 m long. It died out in Argentina around 5370 BC. Its latest remains, at Campo Laborde, show signs of human hunting and butchery. Habitat modelling suggests its suitable range had already shrunk and broken up by the mid-Holocene, so both people and a changing land may have played a part.

nort-018.title: Kikai-Akahoya: the Holocene's biggest eruption
nort-018.text: Pyroclastic flows, avalanches of hot gas and ash, crossed the sea to reach southern Kyushu, up to 100 km away. They came from Japan's submarine Kikai Caldera, in the Akahoya eruption. It was a VEI 7 event, one of only six confirmed eruptions of its size in the Holocene. A 2024 study put the ejecta at 332–457 km³, the largest eruption of the past 11,700 years. Ash fell as far as Hokkaido. Two large earthquakes shook the region during the eruption, and a megatsunami left deposits along western Japan's coast up to 300 km away. It transformed southern Kyushu's vegetation and hit the early Jōmon culture there hard. Recovery took nearly 1,000 years, though local pottery traditions survived.

nort-019.title: The Ilumetsa craters in Estonia
nort-019.text: Two probable meteorite craters, about 80 m and 50 m wide, formed together in southeastern Estonia. The word probable matters. No meteorite fragments or shock features have been found, so their impact origin is likely but not proven.

nort-020.title: Lake Mashū's caldera forms on Hokkaido
nort-020.text: An eruption on Hokkaido created the caldera that now holds Lake Mashū. It is listed at VEI 6, with about 18.6 km³ of material. The sources round its date to around 7,000 years ago. The Smithsonian's Global Volcanism Program gives a calibrated radiocarbon date of 5550 ± 100 BCE, about 500 years older.

nort-022.title: Neoglacial cooling sets in
nort-022.text: About 6,000 years ago, the post-glacial warming trend ended and a long cooling trend began. This is Neoglaciation, the spell after {{ref:nort-008}} when glaciers advanced or re-formed, though it has no single clear start. In East Asia its start coincided with a major weakening of the summer monsoon. In western North America, mountain glaciers that had melted away entirely re-formed shortly before 5000 BP. Orbital models suggest this cooling trend would continue for another 23,000 years.

nort-024.title: The sea stops rising
nort-024.text: Global sea level had been rising steadily since 20,000 years ago. About 6,000 years ago it levelled off, and it has been fairly stable since. The rate of rise fell from over 10 mm a year to under 1 mm, beginning some 4,000 years of near-stable sea level. In places the sea overshot today's level: off Santa Catarina, Brazil, it peaked about 2.1 m above present 5,800–5,000 BP. The last rising water drowned the last land bridges, such as the southern Kuril link to Hokkaido around 6,000 BP.

nort-021.title: The green Sahara dries into desert
nort-021.text: Dust off Mauritania rose sharply within a few centuries. It was a sign that the African humid period, which had kept the Sahara green, was ending. The end came about 6,000–5,000 years ago, often put at 5,500 BP, and the green Sahara began turning into desert. North of the monsoon belt, drying came in one step within 500 years. Orbital shifts cut rainfall and raised temperatures, undoing the changes that had greened the desert in {{ref:gree-015}}. Overgrazing has also been proposed as a trigger. Lakes dried and vegetation vanished. Dust from basins such as Bodélé, now Earth's largest dust source, grew. Shrinking wetlands lowered atmospheric methane. People suffered too. North Africa's population fell within a millennium, and many inner-Arabian settlements were abandoned about 5,300 years ago.

nort-025.title: Pinatubo's Crow Valley eruptions
nort-025.text: Mount Pinatubo's famous 1991 eruption was not its largest. During its earlier Crow Valley eruptive period, it produced pyroclastic flows two to three times larger than those of 1991. That eruption is listed at VEI 6, with about 12 km³ of material.

nort-026.title: The 5.9-kiloyear drought drives herders to the Nile
nort-026.text: Around 3900 BCE, an aridification event, a sharp turn toward drier climate, struck the Sahara. Pastoral herders were forced to migrate into the Nile valley to survive. Farther east, in Hoti Cave in Arabia, the record shows the Indian monsoon retreating southward about 5,900 years ago. The event corresponds to Bond event 4, about 3900 BC, one of eight North Atlantic ice-rafting events. The Sahara's drying may have driven the spread of farming in the Sahel. The desert had re-formed by 3500–3000 BC.

nort-027.title: Mammoths outlast the mainland on St. Paul Island
nort-027.text: A small woolly mammoth population survived on St. Paul Island, Alaska, until about 3750 BC, long after mainland mammoths vanished. People were not to blame: there is no evidence of prehistoric people on the island. Bone dates and environmental records tightly fix their end to around 5,600 years ago. The most likely cause is that fresh water ran short.

nort-028.title: The Piora Oscillation chills the Alps
nort-028.text: Around 5,375 BP a sudden rise of Lake Constance, a sign of cooling, forced people to abandon the Arbon-Bleiche 3 lakeshore village. The Piora Oscillations were two cold periods in Alpine climate history, named after Switzerland's Val Piora. They coincided with the end of the African humid period. From 5,600 to 5,000 years ago, cooling and erratic rainfall were widespread. The Arctic cooled, sea ice spread and Atlantic overturning weakened.

nort-029.title: Ötzi the Iceman dies in the Alps
nort-029.text: About 5,300 years ago a man was killed on the Tisenjoch pass, on today's Austrian–Italian border. Glacier ice at about 3,210 m preserved him as a natural mummy, now known as Ötzi, the oldest known human mummy. He carried both a copper axe and a flint knife. Einkorn and barley grains found beside him reflect the Neolithic farming that had spread into Europe.

nort-031.title: The Morasko craters near Poznań
nort-031.text: Near today's Poznań, Poland, a meteorite fall made a field of seven craters about 5,000 years ago. The largest is about 100 m wide.

nort-032.title: Mount Rainier collapses into the Osceola Mudflow
nort-032.text: About 5,000 years ago, a huge part of Mount Rainier slid away, taking about 490 m off its summit. The debris avalanche fed the Osceola Mudflow, a torrent of mud and rock. It reached the sites of today's Tacoma and south Seattle.

nort-033.title: Burckle crater: a disputed impact
nort-033.text: Beneath the southwest Indian Ocean lies a 29 km undersea feature. The Holocene Impact Working Group proposes that it is an impact crater about 5,000 years old. Its backers link it to floods that affected Sumerian civilization. Other geologists dispute that the Burckle feature is an impact crater at all.

nort-030.title: Iron falls on Campo del Cielo
nort-030.text: Sometime between about 5,000 and 4,000 years ago, a shower of iron meteorites fell on the plains bordering Argentina's Chaco Province. That strewn field is called Campo del Cielo.

nort-034.title: The Henbury crater field in central Australia
nort-034.text: A fragmented meteorite blasted over a dozen craters in central Australia. The field is no older than about 4,700 years. It is one of the few impacts in a populated area and among the best-preserved small crater fields on Earth.

nort-035.title: Cerro Blanco: the Central Andes' largest eruption
nort-035.text: Cerro Blanco in Argentina produced the largest known eruption of the Central Andes. The VEI 7 event formed its youngest caldera and thick ignimbrites. It released about 110 km³ of tephra, the fragments thrown out by an eruption, comparable to the largest Holocene eruptions. That tephra is now a regional time marker. Ground beneath the volcano is still subsiding, which may be a lasting effect of the eruption.
